body: Mats happen. Doodles, cocker spaniels, golden retrievers — any heavy-coated breed can develop matting between grooms, especially after wet walks or growth spurts in young dogs. We don't judge, we just help.
Light matting (small, surface-level tangles) we can usually work through during a normal full groom — we'll add a fee from £10 for the extra time. Brush, conditioner, gentle line-brushing, done.

Moderate matting (firmer, closer to the skin in patches) needs a dedicated de-matting session — from £50. We use de-matting spray and patient line-brushing, working in small sections, with breaks for your dog. This can take an hour or more, depending on coat condition.

Severe matting (pelting — when the coat has felted close to the skin) is harder. Brushing through a heavily pelted coat is genuinely painful for the dog, and not always safe — it can pull on skin and cause sores. The kindest, fastest option is usually a strip-clip down to a short, healthy length and start fresh. We'll always show you what we're seeing, talk it through, and never carry on if your dog is becoming distressed. From £60, often less for smaller dogs.

Either way, you'll leave with a clear plan for keeping the coat right between grooms — usually a more frequent groom cycle, plus a brushing routine that takes 3-5 minutes a day. We're happy to recommend a brush type for your specific coat.

Mats nearly always form in the same handful of places, which is useful to know because it tells you where to brush. The friction points come first: behind and under the ears, around the collar, under a harness and in the armpits where the legs rub the body, the back of the thighs, and the feathering on the legs and belly that drags through wet grass. Movement and moisture do the damage — a coat that gets wet on a walk and then dries while the dog runs, lies down and rolls is being worked into knots all the while. This is why the dogs that mat most are the busy, outdoorsy, water-loving ones with longer coats, not the lazy ones.

The single most useful home habit is to brush down to the skin rather than over the top, and to do it when the coat is dry. A mat starts in the undercoat against the skin, so a brush that only glides over the surface can leave a tidy-looking dog with a layer of felt forming underneath — the mat you cannot see is the one that catches people out. Lift the coat in sections and brush from the roots outwards, and check the friction points by feel with your fingers. One thing to avoid: bathing a matted coat before it is brushed out, because water tightens existing mats and pulls them closer to the skin, turning a workable tangle into a harder job.

If a clip-down is the kindest option, it helps to know what to expect afterwards so it does not come as a shock. The coat will be noticeably shorter than usual and may look or feel different at first — thinner, or a slightly different texture — and skin that has been under a tight mat can be pink or tender for a few days while it gets air and light again. It grows back. Getting it back to a full, healthy length usually takes a few months and a fresh routine: more frequent grooms while it grows through, and a short daily brush with a tool suited to that coat, which we will show you before you leave so the recovery actually sticks.

faqs.q: Will it hurt my dog to remove the mats?
faqs.a: Mild matting, no — it's a slow, gentle process with conditioner. Severe matting, yes — pulling on pelted coat hurts and can damage skin. That's why we offer the strip-clip alternative for badly matted coats. Welfare always wins over aesthetics.

faqs.q: How do I stop matting happening again?
faqs.a: Two things — slightly more frequent grooms (every 5-6 weeks instead of 8), and a daily 3-minute brush with the right tool. We'll show you the tool and the technique before you leave.

faqs.q: Why is de-matting more expensive than a normal groom?
faqs.a: Time, and skill. A normal full groom is 1.5-3 hours. A heavily matted dog can take 2-4 hours plus a recovery period for the skin. The price reflects that — not the difficulty of brushing.

faqs.q: My dog won't stand still to be brushed at home. What do I do?
faqs.a: Start in tiny sessions — 30 seconds, lots of treats, increase gradually. We can talk you through the routine when you come in. Often the issue is the brush type, not the dog.
